notes.5: The majority of stronger candidates identified the limit of proportionality. However, weaker candidates struggled to do this, with a significant number choosing option B.
notes.8: In this question, candidates had to use the equation FΔt = Δmv to calculate the magnitude of the momentum of the ball as it left the tennis racket. Most candidates found this calculation challenging, with only some stronger candidates answering correctly. The most common incorrect answer for weaker candidates was option B, indicating that they only calculated the change in momentum. Some other candidates chose option C, as they did not consider that the direction of the ball reversed after hitting the racket. �PAGE�4
notes.10: This question assessed candidates’ knowledge of energy resources. Most stronger candidates chose the correct answer. However, many weaker candidates had the misconception that the Sun is not the main source of energy for oil.
notes.16: In this question, candidates had to use the relationship pV = constant. Most candidates were confident in using this relationship correctly. The most common incorrect option chosen by weaker candidates was option C. This indicated that they had misread the information in the question and used the value given for the final volume of the gas as the initial volume instead, and then proceeded to calculate a new value for the final volume of the gas. Candidates could benefit from underlining or highlighting numerical data in questions and writing a clear list of each quantity before substituting into equations.
notes.20: This question assessed candidates’ understanding of ultrasound. Nearly all candidates knew that ultrasound has a higher frequency than audible sound, but many weaker candidates had the misconception that ultrasound is a transverse wave.
notes.22: This question about total internal reflection was answered well by stronger candidates who were able to recall the conditions under which the ray of light would be totally internally reflected. Although most weaker candidates knew that the angle of incidence had to be greater than the critical angle, the majority believed that the ray had to be travelling from air into water, and therefore chose option B.
notes.27: In this question, candidates needed to compare the resistances of wires with different lengths and different cross-sectional areas. It appeared that most candidates were aware that as the cross-sectional area doubled, the resistance halved and therefore the length would have to double in order for the resistance of the wire to remain constant. The most common error made by weaker candidates was to choose option C, as they thought that if the cross-sectional area doubled, the length would have to halve.
notes.30: Most stronger candidates were able to use the right-hand rule to correctly determine the direction in which the wire was moved. Although most weaker candidates were able to work out that the movement of the wire was perpendicular to the paper, it appears that they used the left-hand rule instead and therefore chose option D.
notes.38: This question assessed candidates’ knowledge of decay equations. Most stronger candidates identified that a proton was emitted. The majority of weaker candidates incorrectly identified ‘x’ as a beta particle.
notes.39: Candidates demonstrated a very good understanding of the effect of the Earth’s gravitational field on the mass and the weight of an object as the object is moved further away from the Earth’s surface. �PAGE�5
notes.general_comments:
Candidates demonstrated very good knowledge of simple momentum calculations, gas pressure and the
process of evaporation. However, there were some misconceptions about energy resources and total
internal reflection.
It was evident that most candidates struggled with change in momentum calculations and weaker candidates
struggled with calculations involving the combined resistance of resistors in parallel.
